newsitem.title: FRANCE: Car bomb kills seven, wounds 20 by Algeria market.
newsitem.headline: Car bomb kills seven, wounds 20 by Algeria market.

text.p: A car bomb killed at least seven people and wounded 20 on Friday near the market in the Algerian town of Boufarik, security forces said.
The security force statement, carried on the official news agency APS, said the casualty figures were provisional.

Boufarik lies some 20 km (12 miles) south of the capital, which has been the scene of previous bombings blamed on Moslem fundamentalists engaged in a nearly five-year-old conflict to try to topple the authorities.
No more details were immediately available. But the health minister and head of the National Security Service (DGSN) had gone to the scene.
Markets are generally crowded on Friday mornings as Algerians shop ahead of mass Friday prayers.

"The Algerian government reaffirms its determination to combat without respite these criminals and affirms that the enemies of this nation will be pursued and punished for their horrible acts," said a statement from the presidency.
It gave no additional details on the Boufarik bomb attack, saying only that this "cowardly act" showed the "ignoble aims of these criminals and their negation of all human values..."
A series of car bombs have killed hundreds of people, and a government-appointed body said last month that 1,400 people had been killed by bombs in the past two years.
Last weekend, two bombs exploded in two Algerian towns, killing three people and wounding at least 16.

President Liamine Zeroual said on Saturday the security situation had improved this year compared to last three years. But he acknowledged that rebel attacks would not be ended in "one or two months", although 2,000 fundamentalists had given in their weapons and repented.

"Of course, there still remain some problems but the Algerian state has at its disposal all means to wipe out this phenomenon unknown to our society," Zeroual said, describing the guerrillas as "mercenaries, traitors and criminals."
An estimated 50,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
Besides car bombs, a series of bombs have gone off recently in restaurants and cafes.

"They seem to have been targeting police stations and cafes and restaurants patronised by police and security people these past two or three months," said one senior Western diplomat by phone from Algiers on Friday.
"They walk into restaurants and plant a bomb which is often disguised as a portable radio."
